notes_list.title: Electronic Effects — Inductive Effect
notes_list.basic_overview: The sigma-bond polarization transmitted through a carbon skeleton; electron-withdrawing and electron-releasing substituents alter stability, acidity, basicity and reactivity.
notes_list.extra_info_content: +I groups push electron density through sigma bonds; −I groups withdraw it. The effect decreases rapidly with distance. Compare CF3, NO2, CN, halogens, alkyl groups and charged substituents using both magnitude and distance.
notes_list.examples: Acidity: CH3CO2H vs ClCH2CO2H vs CCl3CH2CO2H. Carbocation stability is generally helped by +I groups and harmed by strong −I groups.
notes_list.conditions_and_medium: Polar/protic media can change the observed outcome because solvation may dominate intrinsic electronic effects. Inductive effect is strongest close to the substituent.
notes_list.mechanism_steps: 1. Identify polarized bond. 2. Assign donor/withdrawer. 3. Trace effect through sigma framework. 4. Predict stabilization/destabilization of charge or transition state. 5. Check competing resonance effects.
notes_list.kinetics_and_energy: Not a separate rate law; it changes activation free energy by stabilizing reactant, intermediate or transition state. Use Hammond-type reasoning qualitatively when comparing barriers.
notes_list.selectivity_and_stereochemistry: Used in acidity/basicity ranking, carbocation/carbanion stability and reaction-rate comparisons.
notes_list.common_traps: Do not call every electron-withdrawing effect inductive; resonance requires p-orbital overlap. Halogens are −I but can be +M in aromatic systems.

exam_focus.level: IIT-JAM / MSc entrance / GATE concept depth
